lead: When every main generator is lost, a small air-driven generator called the ram air turbine (RAT) drops into the slipstream and feeds the emergency AC bus. A permanent magnet generator (PMG) supplies engine control power, and the battery bridges the gap until the RAT is online. ETOPS sets how long a twin must survive on one generator plus these backups. Only a few universities teach this at depth.
prereq: You need 3.1 for main sources and 3.3 for battery capacity and usable charge.

blocks.text: Main generators on the engines supply normal power. When all fail, the aircraft still needs instruments, radios, flight controls and engine control. These essential loads sit on the emergency AC bus and the essential DC bus. The chain works in order. Protection removes the failed generators. The RAT deploys. Its generator feeds the emergency AC bus, which feeds an essential transformer rectifier (TRU). The TRU makes 28 V DC for the essential DC bus. The battery carries that DC bus for the few seconds before the RAT is online. The PMG supplies engine control power independently. The emergency AC bus is separate from the main AC buses, so a main-bus fault cannot reach emergency equipment. The essential TRU is sized for these loads only. A contactor connects the battery when the DC bus voltage falls. Each source covers the gap for the next. This order is automatic. The chain is tested.

sections.h3: Ram air turbine, PMG and backup converters

blocks.text: Ram air turbine (RAT): a small propeller on a strut is released into the airstream. It spins a generator of a few kVA (kilovolt-amperes). Deployment is automatic after loss of all AC power, or manual. The RAT has an airspeed band: below the lower limit it turns too slowly, above the upper limit it may overspeed. Inside the band its voltage and frequency still vary with airspeed. It feeds the emergency AC bus, not the main buses. Permanent magnet generator (PMG): a magnet rotor spins inside a fixed stator winding. There is no field winding, so the output cannot be switched off by removing field current; only stopping the shaft stops it. On an engine or APU it supplies control power to the electronic control unit, and in some APUs ignition power during start; on engines the igniters are usually fed from the aircraft AC bus. Its frequency rises with shaft speed, so it is rectified before use. Backup converters let the battery feed the essential DC bus; a static inverter makes AC for the AC standby bus.

ETOPS means Extended-range Twin-engine Operational Performance Standards. It sets the time a twin-engine aircraft may fly from a point on the route to a suitable alternate with one engine inoperative. Common limits are 60, 120 and 180 minutes. The rule is about time, not distance: at 420 kt (knots), 120 minutes is 840 nautical miles (nm), and 180 minutes is 1260 nm. For the electrical system, ETOPS asks whether the remaining generator, the APU start and the battery can carry the essential loads for the diversion time. The battery does not do this alone. It covers the gap until the APU generator or the RAT is online. ETOPS approval checks every source in the chain. Formula: t = Q_usable / I, where t is time in hours, Q_usable is usable charge in ampere-hours and I is current in amperes. Usable charge is less than rated capacity, as the battery chapter 3.3 shows.

spec.title: Emergency supply chain after generator loss
spec.aria: Loss of all generators deploys the ram air turbine, whose small generator feeds the emergency AC bus and an essential transformer rectifier, while the battery bridges the essential DC bus until the RAT is online. The PMG feeds the engine or APU control unit independently of the aircraft buses.

examples.question: An aircraft is cleared for ETOPS 120, so it must stay within 120 minutes of a suitable alternate; at 420 kt that is 840 nm. Its essential DC bus draws 2.8 kW at 28 V. The battery is rated 40 Ah and only 50 % may be used. Find the bus current, usable charge and battery time, and say what this means for the diversion.
steps: Bus current I = P / V = 2800 W / 28 V = 100 A.
Time t = Q_usable / I = 20 Ah / 100 A = 0.2 h.
examples.answer: 100 A, 20 Ah and 12 min; the RAT or APU must take over long before 120 minutes.
examples.check:
distance_nm = 420 * 2
power_W = 2800
voltage_V = 28
current_A = power_W / voltage_V
rated_Ah = 40
usable_fraction = 0.5
usable_Ah = rated_Ah * usable_fraction
time_h = usable_Ah / current_A
time_min = time_h * 60
print(int(distance_nm))
print(int(current_A))
print(int(usable_Ah))
print(int(time_min))

traps: Thinking the battery covers the full ETOPS diversion; it only bridges until the RAT or APU generator is online.
Forgetting the RAT airspeed band; outside it the output is unusable.
Confusing the PMG with a wound-field generator; no field winding means it cannot be switched off electrically.
Using rated battery Ah instead of usable Ah; only a fraction may be discharged.

quiz.q: What does RAT mean and what turns it?
quiz.a: Ram air turbine; a small propeller in the airstream.

quiz.q: Why can a PMG not be switched off by its field?
quiz.a: It has no field winding; only stopping the shaft stops it.

quiz.q: DC bus 1.4 kW at 28 V; battery 30 Ah, 50 % usable. Find current and time.
Why is the battery not sized for the full ETOPS diversion?
quiz.a: It only bridges until the RAT or APU generator is online; those carry the diversion load.

quiz.q: What happens if the RAT is used outside its airspeed band?
quiz.a: Output is too low or the turbine overspeeds; voltage and frequency may be unusable.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern RATs often combine a generator and hydraulic pump. Research looks at lightweight PMGs and fault-tolerant emergency buses. Search 'RAT emergency power' and 'ETOPS electrical load analysis'.
